transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic? What's been going on that made you decide to come see me?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me today. I really appreciate it. I hope I'm not taking time away from people who have, you know, much more serious issues, but... I guess I've just been having a little trouble at work lately. 

I'm a computer support specialist, and, well, I just can't seem to keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore. Even when it's really important, which is a bit embarrassing to admit. Like, I'll start tracing a client's network problem, and ten minutes later I'll realize I've reread the exact same log entries three times, and I still don't know what they actually say. I feel terrible about it, honestly, because I really want to do a good job. 

Does that make sense? I hope I'm explaining it okay.
When did you first notice this difficulty concentrating at work? Was it sudden, or did it develop gradually over time?

Well, um... I guess it really started becoming a major issue about... maybe a year and ten months ago? 

It wasn't exactly out of nowhere, but... well, I'm a little ashamed to admit this, but I was actually let go from my last position right around then. Fired, I mean. I know that probably sounds terrible, and I promise I'm usually a very hard worker! It's just... at my old job, I had all these routines and systems in place that sort of kept me on track, you know? 

When I lost that job, I lost those systems, too. And ever since then, it's just been causing some pretty serious trouble for me. I just haven't been able to adjust without them. 

I hope that doesn't sound like I'm just making excuses? I really am trying my best to get things under control. Does that answer your question okay?
Over this past year and a half or so, have you been feeling down, sad, or depressed most of the time? Or have you noticed changes in your mood beyond just the trouble concentrating?

Oh, um, no. No, I wouldn't say I've been feeling depressed or sad most of the time. 

I mean, obviously, it gets a little discouraging when I mess up at work or fall behind, but... I really try to keep a positive attitude, you know? I definitely don't want to sit around feeling sorry for myself when I know other people have it so much worse. I always try to look on the bright side. 

So, my mood has actually been pretty okay, all things considered. It's really just the focus and keeping my mind on my tasks that's been the big problem. 

I hope that's helpful? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information, so please let me know if I'm not answering your questions properly.

Have you had any recent illnesses, head injuries, or changes in your physical health around the time your concentration problems started? Also, are you currently taking any medications or have you experienced any other physical symptoms like headaches or sleep problems?

Oh, um, no. No, nothing like that at all. I've been really very lucky with my health, thankfully. No head injuries or... or major illnesses, especially not around the time all this started. 

And I'm not taking any medications right now, either. I try to take good care of myself so I don't become a burden on anyone, you know? As for sleep and headaches... well, I sleep pretty well, I think. No unusual headaches or physical problems at all. I feel perfectly healthy physically. 

I hope that's... well, I hope that's a good thing? I mean, obviously I know being healthy is good, but I just want to make sure I'm not leaving out some tiny detail that you might need to know. Did I cover everything you were asking about just now?
Before you lost your job about a year and ten months ago, going back to when you were a child or teenager, did you ever have trouble paying attention or staying focused on tasks, even back then?

Oh, well, um... I suppose if we go all the way back to when I was a kid... I mean, I was a good kid, I promise! I never wanted to be disruptive or anything. 

But, well, my mother actually still jokes about it to this day. She says that back in grade school, my teachers would always write on my report cards that I was a bright boy, but... well, that I never stayed in my seat. And I guess I had a bad habit of blurting out answers in class before I was called on. Oh, and I was always losing my homework, which was just so embarrassing because I really had done it! I'd just somehow misplace it before it was time to turn it in. 

I hope that doesn't make me sound like I was a terrible student? I really did want to do well and please my teachers, I just... I guess I just had a little too much energy back then, and things slipped through the cracks. Does that give you the kind of background you were looking for? I can try to remember more if you need me to.

When you were working at your previous job before you got fired, before you lost those systems and routines you mentioned, were you actually able to concentrate and focus pretty well on your tasks? Or were you already having some of these same attention problems back then, even with those routines in place?

Oh, um... well, at my old job... I mean, I really tried my best there, I did. I was there for a long time, and I had all these little tricks and routines set up to make sure I was doing everything right. 

But, if I'm being completely honest—and I know I shouldn't make excuses—but even back then, it was... it was a bit of a struggle. I had to work so, so hard just to keep those systems going so I wouldn't mess up. But it wasn't until I got fired about a year and ten months ago that things really fell apart. 

Once I lost that job and all the structure that went with it... that's when it became a really serious problem. For this past year and ten months, without those routines to keep me on track, it's just been so much harder to focus or get anything done right. 

I really hope I'm explaining this well enough? I just don't want you to think I wasn't trying at my old job, because I really was. I just... I really need you to know I was putting in the effort. Is that the kind of information you need?

You mentioned having a lot of energy as a kid and blurting things out in class. Do you still find yourself feeling restless or fidgety now as an adult, or do you have trouble sitting still for long periods?

Oh, um... well, I suppose I do still have a bit of that energy, yes. I try very hard to be polite and attentive, especially in meetings or when someone is talking to me. I really don't want to come across as rude or like I'm not listening! 

But... well, if I'm being perfectly honest, it can be a little difficult sometimes. Even when I'm supposed to just sit still and listen, it sort of feels like... like there's a little motor humming right under my skin. It's this urge where I feel like I just need to stand up, or check on something, or move on to the next problem right that very second. I usually try to hide it by just shifting in my chair or maybe tapping my foot very quietly so I don't bother anyone. 

I hope that doesn't make me sound too impatient or unprofessional? I really do value what other people have to say, it's just... my body just wants to keep moving, I guess. Is that normal? Or is that the kind of thing you were asking about?

When you were working at your previous job with all those routines in place, looking back honestly—were you actually able to sit through meetings or focus on detailed work without feeling that restless motor humming underneath your skin? Or was that fidgety feeling still there even back then, just maybe easier to manage because of your systems?

Oh, well... yes, to be completely honest with you, it was still there back then. I really, really tried to keep it under wraps, I promise. But even with all my routines, if I was sitting with a client, or... or even outside of work, like in a chess meeting, I just couldn't stay entirely still. 

My leg would be bouncing under the table, or I'd be clicking a pen over and over... Since I worked in computer support, I usually had these little plastic cable ties around, and I'd catch myself just turning one over and over in my fingers. I honestly wouldn't even realize I was doing it until somebody finally gave me... well, you know, that look. The one that means I'm being a distraction. 

I always felt so awful when that happened, because I never, ever wanted to annoy my clients or my friends! I really hope you don't think I was being disrespectful to them. It's just... keeping my hands or my leg busy was sort of the only way I could keep my brain focused on what they were saying or what I was supposed to be fixing. Does that make sense? I hope I'm giving you the right kind of examples.

When you were in school as a teenager, did you also have that same restless, fidgety feeling you're describing now—that motor humming underneath your skin—or did that mainly start after you lost your job?

Oh, no, it definitely didn't just start after I lost my job. Um... I've actually been like this for as long as I can remember. I really hope that doesn't make me sound like a lost cause or anything! 

But, yes, even way back in grade school... my mother actually still jokes about it sometimes. She says my report cards always had the same kind of notes on them. The teachers would say I was a bright kid—which, you know, I always tried hard to be a good student! But they'd also write that I could never seem to just stay in my seat, or that I'd just blurt out answers without raising my hand. And... well, I was also pretty terrible about losing my homework, even when I had spent all evening doing it. 

I always felt so bad about it, because I really wasn't trying to be disruptive or irresponsible. I just... I couldn't help it. I hope that's not too disappointing to hear? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the full picture, like you asked. Is that helpful?
